newsitem.title: UK: UK building rebound marred by stg, skills shortage.
newsitem.headline: UK building rebound marred by stg, skills shortage.

text.p: After years in the wilderness, British construction appears to have finally entered the promised land of bumper contracts and a booming private sector.

But just as the recovery seems safe after five consecutive quarters of growth, industry leaders are voicing concerns about the strength of the pound and an impending skills shortage which could ignite wage inflation.
A fully fledged turnaround is now under way, helping to erase years of languishing in a recession which saw 500,000 jobs and much-needed skills lost between 1990 and 1995.

Industry leaders see some parallels with the boom times of the 1980s on the private sector side, with commercial and private sector housing leading the dynamic growth figures. The public sector's recovery remains more fragile.
But industry cheer has been marred by the latest threat posed by the strong pound, described by one company boss as the biggest challenge facing the new Labour government since it took power in May.
The pound has rocketed by 35 percent against the mark since August 1996.
"The strength of sterling will have an effect on the industry by early next year," said Sir Martin Laing, president of the Construction Confederation and chairman of John Laing Plc.
"It is hurting exporters and UK manufacturing. If we did start to see redundancies as a result, it could have an effect on consumer confidence and the housing market," he said.

Arend Dickers, an analyst at Salomon Brothers, told Reuters that the sterling threat and interest rate uncertainty in Britain were enough to make him cautious on the sector. "I am underweight in the industry until interest rates stop rising and sterling stabilises."
"Sterling could result in layoffs, which filters through to the housing market eventually," said Dickers.
Another industry analyst said: "If you have sterling going on and on you have to start asking questions about UK industry -- will sterling end up having a softening effect on the economy."
One potential early warning signal is the recent fallback in new building starts, though house prices generally continue to roar ahead.
The industry's skills shortage is also starting to worry bosses.

Laing told a press briefing on Tuesday for the Construction Confederation's quarterly survey that employers were "having difficulty in securing labour, especially bricklayers. It is obviously having an impact. That's why tender prices are rising."

But the shortage is more extensive. Graham Watts, chief executive of the Construction Industry Council, told Reuters demand for engineers and architects was outstripping supply, leading to "a spiralling inflation effect."
The skills shortage is a potential flashpoint for an industry in recovery mode.
Construction output is seen rising four percent this year and next, compared with a measly 0.1 percent in 1996, said the Building Material Producers group in its last survey.
Commercial property is booming, fuelled by leisure and retail developments.

British house prices were up by over 10 percent in the second quarter compared with last year and a number of major contracting contracts are due to come on stream -- the three billioon pounds ($4.9 billion) Channel Tunnel Rail Link, the Millennium projects and Railtrack Plc's decade-long 10 billion pounds rolling investment programme, to name a few.

Public spending commitments could also inject life elsewhere, with Chancellor Gordon Brown's July 2 budget allocating 1.3 billion pounds to be spent on school repairs and 900 million pounds released from council capital receipts to be spent on public housing.
Watts said the key was finding a way of timing major projects so they did not exacerbate staffing shortages which could fuel inflation.
That in turn would raise the pressure for rate rises and bolster the pound further.
"The big worry about such a rapid increase in work is the inflationary effect," said Watts.
"The good news is that this time we have made good strides in productivity and that should partly balance it out -- so the threat of overheating is not as significant as it was in the 80s."
